messages.subject: unbalanced panel with autocorrelation
parts:
Hello,

I am a Stan novice. I am trying to write a model for (unbalanced) panel data that incorporates correlation over time. I have seen there is a not too different question a while ago, but I was not able to adapt it to my case, sorry!

The part I am stuck with is

`
y_it = lambda_it + x_i beta + epsilon_it

lambda_it = (some stochastic autocorrelated process depending on pass lambda_it)
`

where i is the individual, t is the period, and the number of periods varies across individuals (the panel is unbalanced). ;lambda_it are individual effect, x_i are covariates  and epsilon_it is standard normal iid.

Assuming that I don't want to estimate the model in differences, how can I write the dynamic process given that the number of observations varies across units?

I was thinking that perhaps I could create a variable for each unit that would account for the number of observations/periods, and then use a loop in the stan program? What data structure should I use to model the individual effects, given that that 1) I need two indexes (one for the unit/individual, another one for the period) but 2) the panel is unbalanced (not all units have the same number of periods), so the number of iterations would be different for each individual? Can I do this with a two dimensional array?

Thank you in advance

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unbalanced panel with autocorrelation
parts:
The first place to look is the manual chapter on ragged and sparse
data. Until we get ragged arrays, you have to code everything up
in simpler data structures and then slice it out. This is much easier
now with the array slicing (e.g., a[3:7]) than it used to be, but
the manual chapter may not have been updated and may still use older
slicing functions.

If you still have questions after that, let us know and we can help
further.

- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

Sorry for bugging you again. Thanks for your answer (and for the work you have done developing Stan!), I had gone through the manual but did not expect that the answer would be there!

 I have now managed to get the program compiled and running well. Unfortunately, the markov chain does not converge (it is apparent when examining the diagnostics).

Here is my code:
 
    data{

      int<lower = 0> N;// #observations
      int<lower=0> K; // #individuals
      int T[K]; // #observations/periods per individual
      vector[N] y; // observations
    }
    parameters{
      vector[N] x; // latent factor
      real<lower = 0> mu[K];//average
      real<lower = 0> sigma_eta;//variance of temporary shock
      real<lower = 0> sigma_eps;//variance of permanent shock
    }
    model{
      int iter;
      iter = 1; // create an iterator to go through the vector
      for (k in 1:K){//outerloop to iterate through each individual
        //Define initial values for the individual
        x[iter] ~ normal (mu[k], sigma_eta);
        y[iter] ~ normal (x[iter], sigma_eps);
        iter = iter +1;//one step ahead since
   
        for(time_ind in 2:T[k]){//innerloop to iterate through periods
          x[iter] ~ normal (x[iter-1], sigma_eta);//transition equation
          y[iter] ~ normal (x[iter], sigma_eps);// measurement equation
        }
        iter = iter + 1;//jump to next
      }
    }


My guess is that it does not converge because sampling the x[K] factors makes it particularly intensive computationally. The parameters I am truly interested in, however, are sigma_eps and sigma_eta, which I would like to model in a more sophisticated way -based on covariates or period specific- in future stages. Do you have any suggestion? Perhaps re-parametrizing the model in some fashion it would be computationally feasible?

Best,

Luis

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unbalanced panel with autocorrelation
parts:
I don't see the ragged data in your example, so I misunderstood
your first question.

I'm afraid I'm going to recommend the manual again, this
time for non-centered parameterizations. And for efficient
ways to code. But I'll provide some hints inline below.

> On Mar 20, 2017, at 9:04 PM, Luis G <luism....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Sorry for bugging you again. Thanks for your answer (and for the work you have done developing Stan!), I had gone through the manual but did not expect that the answer would be there!
>
> I have now managed to get the program compiled and running well. Unfortunately, the markov chain does not converge (it is apparent when examining the diagnostics).
>
> Here is my code:
>
> data{
>
> int<lower = 0> N;// #observations
> int<lower=0> K; // #individuals
> int T[K]; // #observations/periods per individual
> vector[N] y; // observations
> }
> parameters{
> vector[N] x; // latent factor
> real<lower = 0> mu[K];//average
> real<lower = 0> sigma_eta;//variance of temporary shock
> real<lower = 0> sigma_eps;//variance of permanent shock
> }
> model{
You probably want priors.

> int iter;
> iter = 1; // create an iterator to go through the vector
> for (k in 1:K){//outerloop to iterate through each individual
> //Define initial values for the individual
> x[iter] ~ normal (mu[k], sigma_eta);

You are defining p(x[1] as follows:

p(x[1]) propto PROD_{k in 1:K} normal(x[1] | mu[k], sigma_eta)

This is unlikely to be what you want. If you did want it, you could
vectorize as

x[iter] ~ normal(mu, sigma_eta) if mu is K elements long.

> y[iter] ~ normal (x[iter], sigma_eps);
> iter = iter +1;//one step ahead since
>
> for(time_ind in 2:T[k]){//innerloop to iterate through periods
> x[iter] ~ normal (x[iter-1], sigma_eta);//transition equation
> y[iter] ~ normal (x[iter], sigma_eps);// measurement equation
> }

Now you define x[2] using (T[2] - 2 + 1) different priors, again not
what you probably want.

If you had wanted to do it, a better way to code this for efficiency
is with vectorization:

x[2:T[k]] ~ normal(x[1:(T[k] - 1)], sigma_eta);
> iter = iter + 1;//jump to next
Did you really want to increment iter twice in each loop?
> My guess is that it does not converge because sampling the x[K] factors makes it particularly intensive computationally.

That's part of the problem, but probably not why you think. The problem
here is the measurement model and the fact that you're probably overspecifying
priors here in a way that doesn't make sense.

> The parameters I am truly interested in, however, are sigma_eps and sigma_eta, which I would like to model in a more sophisticated way -based on covariates or period specific- in future stages. Do you have any suggestion? Perhaps re-parametrizing the model in some fashion it would be computationally feasible?

I think you need to sort out the distributions---I don't think they're
right in this specification.

- Bob

messages.author: 29ce8550baceaeb0
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unbalanced panel with autocorrelation
parts:
Hi Luis, 

This model looks pretty poorly identified, so I'd expect bad sampling performance. Do you expect the individuals to be correlated within time periods? If so it might be worth specifying the latent factor model at the level of the hyperprior, then the x_it would be distributed around that. Something like: 

// time an integer[] with the time period, T the number of time periods, N number of observations

parameters {
  vector[N] x;
  vector[T] mu;
// also int, sigma, slope
}
model {

mu[1] ~ prior for starting value

// dynamic model for hyperprior
for(t in 2:T) {
  // I normally use AR(P) models for time-varying parameters, as you 
  // can simulate (many of) them into the future without the process exploding
  // you can also include things like seasonality here by taking fourier transforms of time or whatnot 
  mu[t] ~ normal(int + slope *mu[t-1], sigma);

}

// then your data-level model

for(n in 1:N) {
  // your individual latent parameters are centered around the latent parameters for each time
  x[n] ~ normal(mu[time[n]], some scale parameter with tight prior);
  // your data model
  y[n] ~ normal(x[n], scale); 
}

}


That should probably work better. 

Jim
